authoredPrompt: This figure places two panels side by side, labeled (a) and (b) beneath them, each a shaded three-dimensional cylinder standing on end and representing the same rod under opposite loading. In panel (a) a thick red arrow labeled F points straight up from above the top face and a matching red arrow labeled F points straight down from below the bottom face; a dashed outline extends above the solid cylinder to mark the stretched portion, bracketed at the left as 'Delta L', with a longer bracket below it spanning the original length 'L0'. In panel (b) the two red arrows are reversed, pressing inward from above and below, a curly leader labels the top circular face 'A', and a bracket labeled 'Delta L' at the right runs from the top face down to a dashed ellipse drawn inside the cylinder where the end formerly sat, with 'L0' bracketed at the left. Both cylinders are drawn at identical width, so the whole comparison rests on whether the dashed reference outline lies outside or inside the solid body. The pairing defines the signed length change from the undeformed length L0 that enters tensile and compressive strain, with the cross-section held constant in the low-stress linear range.
authoredInteractions:
- Toggle between tension and compression: the learner switches the loading mode, the red force arrows reverse and the dashed reference moves outside or inside the cylinder, making the sign of Delta L relative to L0 clear.
- Slider for applied force magnitude: the learner drags from compression through zero to tension, the cylinder shortens or lengthens while its cross-section stays fixed, showing the linear low-stress relationship between axial force and length change.
authoredContext:
Tension or compression occurs when two antiparallel forces of equal magnitude act on an object along only one of its dimensions, in such a way that the object does not move. One way to envision such a situation is illustrated in the figure. A rod segment is either stretched or squeezed by a pair of forces acting along its length and perpendicular to its cross-section. The net effect of such forces is that the rod changes its length from the original length L0 that it had before the forces appeared, to a new length L that it has under the action of the forces. This change in length ΔL=L−L0 may be either elongation (when L is larger than the original length L0) or contraction (when L is smaller than the original length L0). Tensile stress and strain occur when the forces are stretching an object, causing its elongation, and the length change ΔL is positive. Compressive stress and strain occur when the forces are contracting an object, causing its shortening, and the length change ΔL is negative.

Compressive stress and strain are defined by the same formulas, the equation and the equation, respectively. The only difference from the tensile situation is that for compressive stress and strain, we take absolute values of the right-hand sides in the equation and the equation.

When an object is in either tension or compression, the net force on it is zero, but the object deforms by changing its original length L0. (a) Tension: The rod is elongated by ΔL. (b) Compression: The rod is contracted by ΔL. In both cases, the deforming force acts along the length of the rod and perpendicular to its cross-section. In the linear range of low stress, the cross-sectional area of the rod does not change.

Figure A is a schematic drawing of a cylinder with a length L0 that is under the tensile strain. Two forces at the different sides of cylinder increase its length by Delta L. Figure B is a schematic drawing of a cylinder with a length L0 that is under the compressive strain. Two forces at the different sides of cylinder reduce its length by Delta L.

discrepancies: The right compression panel is dimmed and semi-transparent in the default view, whereas the source shows both panels with equal visual weight.
Force labels are plain F rather than the vector notation used in the source.
The bottom force labels and panel labels crowd each other, making the lower arrows less faithful to the clean source layout.
The rods are darker and more transparent than the pale opaque blue cylinders in the source, with extra internal/back edges visible especially on panel (b).
The default 3D view is slightly more isometric than the source, making the cylinders look bulkier and less like the textbook schematic.
evaluation.notes: The generated figure is recognizable and conceptually close, but it over-emphasizes interactivity/dimming and has weaker fidelity in labels, opacity, and clean textbook layout.
action_items: Show both tension and compression panels at equal opacity by default to match the side-by-side reference.
Use vector notation for all force labels, e.g. F with an arrow above it.
Move the bottom F labels and (a)/(b) panel labels apart so the lower arrows are clearly readable.
Lighten the rod material and reduce transparency/back-edge visibility to better match the pale textbook cylinders.
